props.title: All About Our House

sections.content: **All About Our House (2001)** (2001) marks a brilliant exploration of Japanese domestic architecture and family dynamics through director Koki Mitani's lens. The film follows a young couple's challenging journey to build their dream home, dealing with an idealistic architect and a traditional carpenter father. It shares thematic DNA with other architecture-focused films like The Lake House (2006) and **Columbus** (2017), but brings a distinctly Japanese perspective on how living spaces reflect cultural values and generational tensions.

sections.content: The film masterfully uses architecture as metaphor for bridging tradition and modernity, a theme that resonates through contemporary Japanese cinema. Like **Tokyo Sonata** (2008) and Still Walking (2008), it examines how physical spaces become battlegrounds for generational values. The conflict between the modernist architect and traditionalist father echoes broader cultural tensions in millennial Japan, similar to those explored in **Departures** (2008).

Mitani's comedic touch distinguishes the film from more serious domestic dramas. His background in theater brings a precise timing to family arguments and construction site chaos. This approach influenced later Japanese films about domestic life like **What the Snow Brings** (2005) and **A Tale of Mari and Three Puppies** (2007), showing how humor can illuminate family dynamics. sections.content: While **All About Our House** (2001) focuses on residential architecture, it belongs to a broader tradition of films exploring how built environments shape human experience. **Inception** (2010) uses architecture as dream manipulation, while **Columbus** (2017) examines how modernist buildings affect emotional connections. These films share an understanding that architecture isn't just background - it's a character that shapes narrative and meaning.
